newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Lissouba sees Kabila after firing between Congos.
newsitem.headline: Lissouba sees Kabila after firing between Congos.

text.p: Congo President Pascal Lissouba made a surprise one-day visit to Laurent Kabila's neighbouring Democratic Republic of the Congo at the weekend, few days after an exchange of shell fire between the two capitals.

Lissouba has blamed the initial shelling from Brazzaville, over the river Congo from Kinshasa, on his predecessor and rival, Denis Sassou Nguesso. A bloody conflict between their rival forces has killed hundreds in Brazzaville since June.
"We don't know where they (the shells) came from," Kabila said on state television late on Saturday.
"I've just spoken about it with my counterpart. It seems that they came from the other side, from Sassou Nguesso's fighters...We're going to find out where they came from."
Lissouba, also on Kinshasa television, accused Sassou of recruiting African mercenaries to foment trouble.

"I promised the president (Kabila) to bring evidence that his opponents, Rwandans who were responsible for the genocide in Rwanda, Ugandan opponents as well as Central African Republic mutineers, are being recruited by this man," Lissouba said after Saturday's talks.
"I think he wants to set fire to and shed blood in Central Africa," Lissouba said.
Presidential elections in Congo-Brazzaville were postponed because of the fighting between the two would-be candidates.
Renewed fighting in Brazzaville has forced thousands of people to flee the capital over the past week.
Peace talks have stalled in Libreville, capital of Gabon, but are expected to resume on Monday, diplomats said.
The Congolese delegations are back in Gabon after several days of consultations with their leaders in Brazzaville.
Lissouba conceded that the talks were getting bogged down, and suggested that the mediation efforts of UN special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun might not be able to take them further.
He appealed for a regional solution to the crisis.

"He (Kabila) is going to get involved. He will not be alone. We would like to see all of Central Africa get involved, because this problem is African, and African problems should preferably be resolved by Africans," he said.
Kabila said an African peacekeeping force should be set up to stop the conflict.
"We think that we must have an African peacekeeping force so that normal life can resume, constitutional life," he said, without elaborating.
The United Nations has backed the idea of an African peacekeeping force but wants a real end to hostilities before it is sent in.
Lissouba also said he would ask neighbouring Central African countries to provide monitors when the presidential election was finally held.
